title: Internet Basics & Online Safety
subtitle: Use your smartphone to get online, save data, communicate by email and protect your accounts, money and privacy from scams.
description: A practical, phone-first course for first-time and growing internet users in Nigeria. You will learn how the internet and data bundles work, how to browse, search and use email well, and how to lock down your accounts with strong passwords, passkeys and two-step verification. You will also learn to spot phishing and SIM-swap scams, install apps safely and use Drive and video calls with confidence.
outcomes: Make a data bundle last longer using Android, WhatsApp, YouTube and Play Store data-saving settings
Search effectively and tell a real website from a fake one by reading its web address
Set up and use a Gmail account professionally, and spot and report phishing emails and SMS
Protect your accounts with a passphrase, a password manager, passkeys and two-step verification
Use Wi-Fi safely, install apps only from trusted sources and set privacy controls on your phone and apps
Recognise a SIM-swap attack and follow an emergency plan to protect your money
audience: Women who are new to the internet or use a smartphone mainly for calls and WhatsApp, and want to go online confidently and safely.
tools: An Android smartphone (an iPhone also works; menu names differ slightly)
A SIM with a data bundle, or access to trusted Wi-Fi
A Google (Gmail) account, created in Module 2 if you do not have one
A notebook and pen for passwords, backup codes and emergency numbers

modules.title: Getting online with your smartphone
modules.overview: Understand what the internet really is, how your phone connects to it through mobile data or Wi-Fi, and how to make every data bundle last longer. Then learn to use a browser, search well and read a web address so you can tell a real website from a fake one.

lessons.title: What the internet is and how your phone connects to it
objectives: Explain the internet and the World Wide Web in plain words
Describe how a message travels from your phone to another person
Tell the difference between mobile data and Wi-Fi
Read the signal and network icons at the top of your phone screen

blocks.text: The **internet** is a huge network of computers and devices all over the world, joined together so they can send information to one another. Your smartphone is one of those devices. When you send a WhatsApp voice note, watch a video or check your bank balance, your phone is sending and receiving small pieces of information, called **data**, through this network.

blocks.name: online-world
blocks.alt: A woman surrounded by connected icons of the world
blocks.caption: Your phone is one small part of a worldwide network of connected devices.

blocks.text: The internet and the Web are not the same thing

People often use the two words for one thing, but they are different. The **internet** is the network itself: the cables, masts, satellites and powerful computers called **servers** that store information. The **World Wide Web** is one service that runs on the internet: the pages you open in a browser, like a news site or a school portal. The Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989. WhatsApp, email and online banking apps also use the internet, but they are not web pages.

head: The internet
The World Wide Web
rows: The network: cables, masts, satellites, servers
Pages and websites you open in a browser
Carries WhatsApp, email, apps, calls and the Web
Is only one of the things the internet carries
Like the roads that join towns
Like the shops you visit using those roads

blocks.text: How your message travels

When you send a photo to your sister in another state, the photo is broken into many small packets. Your phone sends them by radio waves to the nearest **mast** (base station) of your network, such as MTN, Airtel or Glo. From the mast, the packets travel through cables to your network's computers, then across the internet to WhatsApp's servers, and back down to your sister's network and her phone. Her phone puts the packets back together into the photo. All of this usually happens in a second or two.

Much of the internet traffic between Africa and the rest of the world travels through **undersea cables** laid along the ocean floor. Several of these cables land in Lagos, including Google's Equiano cable. This is why a damaged undersea cable can make the internet slow across many countries at once, even when your own phone and network are fine.

No single person or company owns the internet. Each part is owned by someone different: your network owns its masts, cable companies own the cables, and companies like Google or Meta own their servers. A company that sells you access, such as a mobile network or a home broadband provider, is called an **internet service provider (ISP)**. When the internet is down, it is usually one part of this chain, not the whole internet.

blocks.title: From your phone to hers
items: Your phone
Nearest network mast
Network and undersea cables
WhatsApp servers
Her network mast
Her phone
blocks.caption: Every message hops through masts, cables and servers before it reaches the other person.

blocks.text: Two ways your phone gets online

items: **Mobile data**: your SIM card connects to your network's masts. You pay for it with a data bundle. It works almost anywhere there is network coverage.

**Wi-Fi**: your phone connects by radio to a nearby router, for example at home, in an office, a church or a hotel. The router itself is connected to the internet. Wi-Fi does not use your data bundle, but someone pays for that connection.

blocks.text: Look at the top of your screen. The bars show how strong your network signal is. Letters next to the bars show the type of mobile connection: **2G or E** is very slow and mostly good for calls and SMS, **3G or H+** is usable for WhatsApp messages, **4G or LTE** is good for video, and **5G** is faster still where it is available. A fan-shaped Wi-Fi symbol means you are connected to Wi-Fi instead.

blocks.title: When pages will not load
blocks.text: First check the icons. No bars or an E means weak coverage: move near a window or outdoors. Then turn Airplane mode on for ten seconds and off again. This makes your phone search again for the strongest mast nearby.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the icons before a meeting
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna has a WhatsApp video call with her cooperative at 4pm. At 3:50pm her screen shows one bar and the letter E.
steps: She knows E means a very slow 2G connection, too slow for video.
She walks to the front of the compound, where her screen now shows three bars and 4G.
She turns off Wi-Fi because the neighbour's Wi-Fi she once joined is weak and keeps dropping.
She joins the call and switches her own camera off to keep the call steady.
blocks.result: By reading two small icons and moving 20 metres, Halima turned an impossible video call into a clear one.

blocks.text: Words you will meet in this course

items: **App**: a program you install on your phone, such as WhatsApp or your bank app.
**Browser**: an app for opening websites, such as Chrome.
**Account**: your personal space on a service, opened with a username and password.
**Download**: bringing something from the internet onto your phone. **Upload**: sending something from your phone to the internet.

takeaways: The internet is the network; the Web is the pages you open in a browser.
Messages travel as small packets through masts, cables and servers.
Your phone gets online through mobile data (your bundle) or Wi-Fi (a router).
The icons at the top of the screen tell you signal strength and connection type.

activity.title: Map your own connection
steps: Open your phone and write down the network name and the letters shown next to the signal bars (E, 3G, 4G, LTE or 5G).
Check three places: inside your room, at the door and outside. Note the bars and letters in each place.
Turn Airplane mode on for ten seconds and off again, then note whether the letters change.
Write one sentence explaining the difference between the internet and the Web in your own words.
activity.evidence: A short note listing the three places with their signal bars and connection letters, plus your one-sentence explanation.

lessons.title: Data bundles: what you pay for and how to save data
objectives: Explain what MB and GB mean and which activities use the most data
Check your data balance and choose a bundle that fits your use
Turn on data-saving settings in Android, WhatsApp and YouTube
Stop apps from quietly using data in the background

blocks.text: Data is measured in **megabytes (MB)** and **gigabytes (GB)**. One GB is about 1,000 MB (networks usually count 1,024 MB as 1 GB). A data bundle gives you a fixed amount of data that must be used before it expires, for example within a day, a week or 30 days. When it runs out or expires, your phone either stops browsing or starts charging your airtime at a higher rate, depending on your network and settings.

blocks.name: mobile-app-data
blocks.alt: A person looking at data use on a large phone screen
blocks.caption: Knowing which apps use your data is the first step to making a bundle last.

blocks.text: What uses a lot of data and what uses little

head: Activity
Data use
Why
rows: Video calls, YouTube, TikTok, Facebook videos
Moving pictures are the heaviest content
Updates can be hundreds of MB each

blocks.text: Exact amounts change with picture quality and the app, so treat any number you hear as a rough guide. The rule that never changes: **video uses the most data, and higher video quality uses much more**. Watching a video in low quality can use a small fraction of what the same video uses in HD.
Check your balance the safe way

Every network has a short USSD code to check data balance, and an official app (for example the MyMTN or MyAirtel app). Find the correct code on your network's official website or on the back of your SIM pack, and save it in your contacts as "Data balance". Buy bundles only through the official USSD menu, the network's app or your bank app. Never pay a stranger on social media who promises "cheap 50GB for 1,000 naira": this is a common scam.
Five settings that save data

items: **Android Data Saver**: open Settings, search for "Data Saver" and turn it on. It stops most apps from using data in the background. The exact menu name differs between phone brands, so use the search box at the top of Settings.

**WhatsApp media download**: in WhatsApp go to Settings, then Storage and data, then Media auto-download. Set "When using mobile data" to download nothing, or photos only. You can still tap any video to download it when you choose.
**WhatsApp calls**: in the same Storage and data menu, turn on "Use less data for calls".
**YouTube quality**: while a video plays, tap the settings (gear) icon, then Quality, and choose Data saver or a low number such as 360p.
**Play Store updates**: open Play Store, tap your profile picture, then Settings, Network preferences, and set Auto-update apps to "Over Wi-Fi only".

blocks.title: Where your data goes
items: Video and video calls
Updates and downloads
Photos and browsing
Voice notes
Text messages
blocks.caption: Data use grows from the narrow top for text to the wide base for video, so control video first.

blocks.title: Find the data eater
blocks.text: On Android, open Settings and search for "Data usage" or "Mobile data usage". You will see a list of apps with how much each used this month. Restrict background data for any app you rarely use.

blocks.title: Worked example: making a bundle last a month
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha buys a 30-day bundle of about 6GB (price varies by network, roughly a few thousand naira) but it keeps finishing in two weeks.
steps: She opens Mobile data usage and sees Facebook used about 2.5GB and Play Store updates used about 1GB.
In the Facebook app media settings she sets videos to autoplay only on Wi-Fi, and sets Play Store to update over Wi-Fi only.
She sets WhatsApp to download photos only on mobile data, and turns on Android Data Saver.
She saves updates for Sunday, when she uses the free Wi-Fi at her church office.
blocks.result: The next month her bundle lasts the full 30 days, and she has about 1GB left over on the last day.

blocks.title: Auto-renew and "borrowed" data
blocks.text: Some plans renew automatically and take money from your airtime. Some networks also offer data on credit that is repaid from your next recharge. Read the confirmation SMS after every purchase so you know the expiry date and whether it will renew.
Choosing the right bundle

Look at your Data usage screen at the end of a month to see how much you really used. If you used about 3GB, a 30-day plan a little above that is usually cheaper per GB than buying many daily plans. Daily and weekly plans suit people who only go online now and then. Night plans can be cheap, but they only help if you can download things late at night, such as course videos or updates.
Finally, remember that Wi-Fi can save data, but only use trusted Wi-Fi. You will learn in Module 3 why free public Wi-Fi needs extra care, especially for banking.

takeaways: 1 GB is about 1,000 MB; video is by far the heaviest use of data.
Check balance and buy bundles only through official codes, apps or your bank app.
Turn on Data Saver, limit WhatsApp auto-download and set updates to Wi-Fi only.
The Data usage screen shows exactly which app is eating your bundle.

activity.title: Data diet for your phone
steps: Open Settings and find the Data usage screen. Write down the three apps that used the most data this month.
Turn on Android Data Saver.
In WhatsApp, set Media auto-download on mobile data to photos only or no media.
Set Play Store auto-update to Over Wi-Fi only.
Save your network's official data balance code in your contacts.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your Data usage screen and a note of the four settings you changed.

lessons.title: Using a browser and searching like an expert
objectives: Open, use and close tabs in Chrome on a smartphone
Write search words that bring useful results quickly
Use search tools such as quotation marks, site: and voice or Lens search
Judge whether a search result is trustworthy before you rely on it

blocks.text: A **browser** is the app you use to open websites. On most Android phones it is **Google Chrome**. Other browsers include Samsung Internet, Opera Mini and Firefox, and iPhones come with Safari. They all work in a similar way. At the top is the **address bar**, where you can type either a web address (like jamb.gov.ng) or a question you want to search.

blocks.name: mobile-browsers
blocks.alt: A large phone showing a browser window
blocks.caption: Chrome and other browsers all share the same basic parts: address bar, tabs and menu.

blocks.text: The parts of a phone browser

items: **Address bar**: type a web address or search words here.
**Tabs**: each open page is a tab. The square with a number shows how many tabs are open. Tap it to switch or close tabs. Many open tabs slow the phone down.
**Back arrow**: your phone's back button or gesture takes you to the previous page.
**Menu (three dots)**: new tab, history, downloads, bookmarks, settings and Incognito tab.
**Bookmark (star)**: saves a page you will need again, such as your bank's website or your child's school portal.

blocks.title: Incognito is not invisible
blocks.text: An Incognito tab does not save your history on the phone. It does not hide what you do from your network, your employer's Wi-Fi or the websites you visit. Use it on a shared phone, not as a safety tool.
How to search well

A search engine such as **Google** looks through billions of web pages and lists the ones it thinks match your words. The more precise your words, the better the results. Type the important words, not a whole long sentence, and add your location when it matters.

head: Instead of this
Type this
Why it works
rows: how can I know if my NIN is linked to my line
Quotation marks keep the exact phrase together
site: shows results only from that official website
A minus sign removes results with that word

items: **Voice search**: tap the microphone in the Google search bar and speak in English or another supported language.
**Google Lens**: tap the camera icon in the Google search bar and point at a plant, a product label or printed text. Lens can search what it sees and can translate or copy printed words.
**Tools and tabs**: under the search box, tap Images, News or Videos to change the type of results.

blocks.text: Is this result trustworthy?

The top results are not always the best. Some are adverts, marked **Sponsored**, which someone paid for. Scammers sometimes buy adverts that copy real brands. Before you rely on any page, check three things: who runs it, whether the web address matches the organisation, and whether two other trusted sources say the same thing. For government matters in Nigeria, official sites usually end in **.gov.ng**.

blocks.title: Before you trust a result
items: Not a Sponsored advert
Address matches the organisation
Author or owner is clear
Date is recent
Two sources agree
blocks.caption: Run every important search result through these five checks before acting on it.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding the real exam portal
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Abeokuta wants to check her son's exam result. She searches "exam result checker" and the first result is a Sponsored link asking for a 3,500 naira "processing fee" through bank transfer.
steps: She notices the Sponsored label and that the address is a strange mix of letters, not the exam body's own website.
She searches again with the exam body's name and the word "official", and checks that the address matches the organisation's name.
She confirms the same address on the printed registration slip.
She bookmarks the official page with the star in Chrome's menu.
blocks.result: Bisi avoided paying a fake fee and saved the real portal for next time.

blocks.title: Save data while browsing
blocks.text: Close tabs you are not using, avoid autoplaying videos on news sites, and bookmark pages instead of searching for them again every time.
Keeping your browser tidy and safe

Browsers collect history, saved passwords and small files called **cookies** that remember your logins and settings. On your own phone this is convenient. On a shared or borrowed phone, always sign out of accounts and clear history: in Chrome tap the three dots, then History, then Delete browsing data. Keep Chrome updated through the Play Store, because updates fix security holes.

Some websites ask to send you notifications. If you tap Allow by mistake, the site can push adverts and fake virus warnings to your phone even when Chrome is closed. To stop them, open Chrome, tap the three dots, then Settings, Notifications, and switch off any site you do not recognise. A browser should never ask you to install an app to "clean" your phone; that is a scam.

takeaways: The address bar accepts both web addresses and search words.
Short, precise words with a place or exact phrase give better results.
Use site:, quotation marks, the minus sign, voice search and Google Lens.
Skip Sponsored results for important tasks and check the web address.

activity.title: Search challenge
steps: Open Chrome and open two tabs, then close one using the tab button.
Search for the official website of your state government using the word "official" and check that it ends in .gov.ng.
Search for one fact using site: with an official website, for example site:nafdac.gov.ng registration.
Use Google Lens on a product label at home and note what it found.
Bookmark one page you will use often.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your site: search and your Google Lens result, plus a list of your bookmarks.

lessons.title: Reading web addresses, HTTPS and spotting fake websites
objectives: Name the parts of a web address and find the real domain
Explain what HTTPS protects and what it does not
Spot common tricks used in fake website addresses
Check a link safely before you open it

blocks.text: Every web page has an address, called a **URL**. Learning to read it is one of the most powerful safety skills on the internet, because fake websites can copy the look of a real bank or company perfectly, but they cannot use the real company's address.

blocks.name: secure-server
blocks.alt: A padlock beside a web server
blocks.caption: A secure connection protects data on the way, but only the address tells you who you are talking to.

blocks.text: The parts of a web address
Take this example: **https://www.example.com.ng/account/login**. It has four parts:

items: **https://** is the method of connection. The s means the connection is encrypted.
**www.** is a subdomain, an optional part at the front.
**example.com.ng** is the **domain**, the name the owner registered. This is the part that tells you who owns the site.
**/account/login** is the path, the page inside that site.

blocks.text: The rule to remember: **read the domain just before the first single slash**. Look at the last part before that slash. In "example.com.ng.secure-login.xyz/" the real domain is secure-login.xyz, not example. Scammers put a famous name at the front so it looks right at a glance.
Common endings you will see

head: Ending
Usually means
rows: A Nigerian website (company, shop or person)
Often an organisation or charity, but anyone can register it
International commercial, but anyone can register it

blocks.text: What HTTPS does and does not do

**HTTPS** encrypts the information travelling between your phone and the website, so people on the same Wi-Fi or network cannot read it. Browsers warn you with "Not secure" when a page uses plain HTTP. In 2023 Chrome replaced the old padlock symbol with a small settings-style icon, because many people believed the padlock meant a site was trustworthy. It never meant that. **A scam website can have HTTPS too.** HTTPS tells you the line is private; it does not tell you who is on the other end.

blocks.title: What HTTPS proves
items: HTTPS does
HTTPS does not
blocks.caption: Treat HTTPS as necessary for logging in, but never as proof that a website is genuine.

blocks.text: Tricks used in fake addresses

items: **Look-alike spelling**: letters swapped or added, such as "0" for "o", or an extra word like "-verify" or "-ng-update".
**Wrong ending**: the real name with a different ending, such as .net or .xyz instead of the real one.
**Famous name in front**: the brand name at the start, with the real domain hidden at the end.
**Shortened links**: services like bit.ly hide the real address until you open them.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking a link in an SMS
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Port Harcourt receives an SMS: "Your account will be blocked today. Update your BVN at https://gtbank-ng-update.com/verify". She banks with that bank.
steps: She does not tap the link. She presses and holds it to copy it and reads the address instead.
She finds the domain before the first single slash: gtbank-ng-update.com. It is not her bank's official domain.
She opens her bank's official app, which she installed from Play Store, and sees no warning there.
She calls the customer care number printed on the back of her ATM card to report the SMS, then deletes it.
blocks.result: Grace confirmed it was a fake site by reading the domain, and never typed her details anywhere.

blocks.title: Type it or bookmark it
blocks.text: For banking, government portals and anything involving money, do not use links from messages. Type the address you know or use a bookmark you saved yourself, or use the official app.

If you are unsure about a link someone sent on WhatsApp, press and hold it to see the full address. When it is a shortened link, ask the sender what it is, and if the sender is a stranger, simply do not open it.
Signs that a shopping or job website is fake

items: Prices far below every other seller, for phones, generators or foodstuff.
Payment only by direct transfer to a personal account, with no card payment or pay-on-delivery option.
No physical address, or an address you cannot find on a map, and only a WhatsApp number for contact.
A countdown timer or message saying the offer ends in minutes, to rush you.
A job that asks you to pay a "registration" or "training" fee before you are hired.

blocks.text: When you see two or more of these signs, stop. Search the business name with the word "scam" or "review", ask someone you trust, and remember that a real business will still be there tomorrow.

blocks.title: QR codes are links too
blocks.text: A QR code is just a web address in picture form. When your camera reads one, it shows the address before opening it. Read the domain the same way before you tap, especially on posters or stickers in public places.

takeaways: The domain just before the first single slash tells you who owns the site.
HTTPS means a private connection, not an honest website.
Look-alike spelling, wrong endings and hidden domains are common tricks.
For money matters, type the address, use a bookmark or use the official app.

activity.title: Domain detective
steps: Write down the web addresses of three organisations you use: your bank, your network and one government site.
For each one, underline the domain before the first single slash.
Open each in Chrome and tap the icon to the left of the address to see the connection details.
Invent two fake versions of your bank's address using the tricks in this lesson, and explain how you would spot each.
activity.evidence: A page of notes with the three real domains underlined and your two fake examples with explanations.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes the World Wide Web?
options: It is the network of cables and masts
It is the pages and websites you open in a browser, which run on the internet
It is another name for WhatsApp
It is a type of SIM card
quiz.explain: The internet is the network. The Web is one service on it: the pages you open in a browser.

quiz.q: Funmi's bundle keeps finishing early. Her Data usage screen shows YouTube used the most. What should she do first?
options: Buy a bigger bundle every week
Set YouTube to Data saver or 360p quality
Turn off WhatsApp messages
Restart the phone every day
quiz.explain: Video is the heaviest use of data, and lowering video quality saves the most.

quiz.q: In the address https://firstbank.com.ng.account-verify.top/login, what is the real domain?
options: firstbank.com.ng
account-verify.top
https
login
quiz.explain: Read the last part before the first single slash. The famous name at the front is a trick.

quiz.q: A website shows HTTPS. What does that tell you?
options: The website is owned by a real company
The website cannot be a scam
The connection between your phone and the site is encrypted
The website is approved by the government
quiz.explain: HTTPS protects data on the way. Scam sites can use HTTPS too.

quiz.q: Which search will most likely show only results from NAFDAC's own website?
options: NAFDAC information please
registration site:nafdac.gov.ng
"registration" NAFDAC -site
nafdac registration Sponsored
quiz.explain: The site: operator limits results to the website you name.

quiz.q: Your phone shows the letter E next to one bar. What does it most likely mean for a video call?
options: The call will be very clear
The connection is very slow 2G, so move to get a better signal
You are on Wi-Fi
Your data bundle has expired
quiz.explain: E is an old, slow 2G connection. Moving to a spot with 4G or LTE is the fix.

modules.title: Email: set it up, use it well, spot the traps
modules.overview: Create a Gmail account with a professional address and recovery options, then send, organise and find emails on your phone. Learn to write emails that get answered, and to recognise phishing emails and SMS before they cost you money.

lessons.title: Creating a Gmail account with a professional address
objectives: Create a Gmail account on an Android phone or in a browser
Choose a professional email address that is easy to share
Add a recovery phone number and recovery email
Explain what your Google account unlocks beyond email

blocks.text: Email is still how schools, employers, banks, government portals and online courses send official messages. Many services, including WODDI Institute, ask for an email address when you register. **Gmail** is a free email service from Google. One Google account gives you Gmail, the Play Store, Google Drive, Google Photos, YouTube and Google Meet, all with the same email and password.

blocks.name: personal-email
blocks.alt: A woman with an envelope and an email screen
blocks.caption: A Google account gives you an email address plus access to many other Google services.

blocks.title: You may already have one
blocks.text: Every Android phone asks for a Google account to use the Play Store. Open Settings, then Accounts (or Passwords and accounts) to see if one is already on your phone. If someone else set up the phone, make sure the account is yours and you know the password.
Choosing your address

Your Gmail username can be 6 to 30 characters long and can use letters, numbers and full stops. Gmail ignores full stops, so adaeze.okafor@gmail.com and adaezeokafor@gmail.com reach the same inbox. Choose something you will be happy to write on a CV or a business card.

head: Good choice
Avoid
Why
rows: Your name looks professional; nicknames do not
A trade word helps people remember you; random numbers do not
Short addresses are easier to type correctly

blocks.text: Steps to create the account

items: Open the Gmail app and tap your profile picture, then Add another account, then Google. Or open Chrome and go to accounts.google.com and tap Create account. Choose For my personal use.
Enter your first name and surname as they appear on your ID, because some services check this.
Enter your date of birth. Google requires account holders to meet a minimum age, which is 13 in most countries. Gender can be set to Rather not say.
Choose one of the suggested addresses or tap Create your own Gmail address and type yours. If it is taken, add a trade word or town.
Create a strong password of at least 8 characters. You will learn exactly how to make one in Module 3, Lesson 1.
Add your phone number when asked. Google uses it to send codes and to help you get back in if you forget your password.
Read the privacy and terms summary, then tap I agree.

blocks.title: Account set-up order
items: Choose professional address
Create strong password
Add recovery phone
Add recovery email
Run Security Checkup
blocks.caption: Finish all five steps on the first day, not after something goes wrong.

blocks.text: Recovery details: your spare key

Most people lose access to email because they forget the password or lose the phone, not because of hackers. Recovery details let Google confirm it is really you. After creating the account, open **myaccount.google.com**, tap Security, and check that **Recovery phone** and **Recovery email** are filled in. A recovery email can be an older address or a trusted family member's email.

blocks.title: Never use someone else's account
blocks.text: Do not let a phone seller or business centre attendant create your account with their own phone number or keep your password. Whoever controls the recovery number can take the account away from you.

blocks.title: Worked example: a clean start
blocks.context: For example, Chidinma in Enugu is applying for a WODDI Institute course. A business centre created her old Gmail years ago, and she no longer knows the password or the phone number used.
steps: She decides to create a new account herself in Chrome at accounts.google.com.
The address chidinma.eze@gmail.com is taken, so she chooses chidinma.eze.enugu@gmail.com.
She adds her own MTN number as the recovery phone and her sister's email as recovery email.
She opens myaccount.google.com, taps Security Checkup and follows each suggestion until it shows a green tick.
She writes the new address clearly in her notebook and sends a test email to her sister.
blocks.result: Chidinma now has an account she fully controls, with two ways to recover it, ready for her course registration.

blocks.text: Adding the account to your phone

If you created the account in a browser, add it to the Gmail app so messages arrive on your phone. In Gmail tap your profile picture, then Add another account, then Google, and sign in. You can keep a personal and a business account side by side and switch between them by tapping your picture.
Google may delete accounts that have not been used for two years. Sign in at least once in a while, even to an account you keep only for backups.

If you run a business, consider a second Gmail account just for customers and suppliers. Keeping business mail separate from family and personal mail makes it easier to find receipts, and you can hand that account to a helper later without exposing your private messages.

takeaways: One Google account opens Gmail, Play Store, Drive, Photos, YouTube and Meet.
Choose a short, professional address based on your name or trade.
Add a recovery phone and recovery email on day one.
Never let someone else's phone number control your account.

activity.title: Set up or check your Gmail
steps: If you have no Gmail, create one following the steps in this lesson. If you have one, open it.
Open myaccount.google.com, tap Security and confirm your recovery phone and recovery email.
Run Security Checkup and follow every suggestion.
Send a test email to a friend and ask them to reply.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of the Security Checkup page with no warnings, and the reply email from your friend.

lessons.title: Sending, receiving and organising email on your phone
objectives: Write and send an email with To, Cc, Bcc and an attachment
Reply, reply all and forward correctly
Organise your inbox with archive, star, labels and tabs
Find any old email quickly with Gmail search

blocks.text: The Gmail app shows your **inbox**, the list of emails you have received, with the newest at the top. Unread messages are in bold. Tap a message to open it. To write a new email, tap **Compose**, the pencil button at the bottom right.

blocks.name: mobile-inbox
blocks.alt: A phone showing a list of emails in an inbox
blocks.caption: A tidy inbox on your phone means you never miss an important message.

blocks.text: The parts of a new email

head: Field
What it is for
Example
rows: The main person you are writing to
People who should know, but do not need to act
Hidden recipients; others cannot see their addresses
A list of customers getting a price update
A short title that says what the email is about
Application: Fashion Design Course, Amina Bello

blocks.title: Use Bcc for groups
blocks.text: When you email many customers or members who do not know each other, put their addresses in Bcc. This protects their privacy and stops one person's reply-all from reaching everyone.
Attaching files and photos

items: In a new email, tap the paperclip icon at the top.
Choose Attach file to pick a document or photo from your phone, or Insert from Drive to share a file stored in Google Drive.
Check the attachment name appears at the bottom of the email before you send.
Gmail attachments can be up to 25 MB. Larger files are sent as a Google Drive link automatically.

blocks.text: Before you attach a scanned document, rename it clearly, for example **Amina_Bello_CV.pdf**, not IMG_20260512.jpg. To turn paper into a clean PDF, open the Google Drive app, tap the plus button and choose Scan.
Reply, reply all or forward?

items: **Reply** answers only the person who sent the email. Use this most of the time.
**Reply all** answers the sender and everyone in To and Cc. Use it only when everyone needs your answer.
**Forward** sends the email to someone new. Delete other people's phone numbers or private details before forwarding.

blocks.title: Undo send
blocks.text: After you tap Send, Gmail shows Undo at the bottom of the screen for a few seconds. Tap it if you notice a mistake or a missing attachment.
Keep your inbox under control

items: **Archive** removes an email from the inbox without deleting it. It stays in All mail and appears in search. Swipe the email left or right to archive.
**Star** marks emails you must come back to. Find them under Starred in the menu.
**Labels** work like folders. On the web version you can create labels like Customers or School; on the phone, open an email, tap the three dots and choose Change labels.
**Tabs**: Gmail sorts mail into Primary, Promotions and Social, so adverts do not bury important messages. Check Promotions occasionally, because real messages sometimes land there.

blocks.title: Daily inbox routine
items: Open new mail
Reply or act
Star if waiting
Archive when done
blocks.caption: Handle each email once: act on it, star it, or archive it, so the inbox shows only what still needs you.

blocks.text: Finding old emails
Type in the search box at the top. Gmail also understands short commands: **from:** a sender, **has:attachment** for emails with files, and **subject:** for words in the subject line.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding an old receipt
blocks.context: For example, Kemi runs a small catering business in Ibadan. Her customer says she paid for a 50-plate order in March, and Kemi needs to find the receipt the payment platform emailed her.
steps: She opens Gmail and types: from:paystack has:attachment in the search box.
Gmail lists about a dozen emails. She scrolls to March and finds the receipt with the customer's name.
She stars it and forwards it to the customer, deleting her own account details from the forwarded text first.
She creates a label called Receipts on the web version and adds future receipts to it.
blocks.result: Kemi found the proof in under a minute instead of scrolling through hundreds of emails.

blocks.text: Turn on notifications only for the account and tabs that matter to you: in Gmail go to Settings, choose your account, then Notifications. This saves battery and stops constant buzzing from promotional mail.
Clearing out promotions and saving space

Your free Google account comes with 15 GB of storage, shared between Gmail, Google Drive and Google Photos. Large attachments and years of promotional mail slowly fill it, and when it is full you cannot receive new email. To make space, search for **has:attachment larger:10M** to find big emails and delete the ones you no longer need. Open the Promotions tab, select old adverts and delete them in one go.

To stop a shop or website from emailing you, open one of its emails and look for the **Unsubscribe** link near the sender name or at the very bottom. Unsubscribe only from companies you recognise. For unknown senders, use Report spam instead, because clicking links in scam emails tells the sender your address is active.

takeaways: To is for action, Cc is for information, Bcc hides addresses in group emails.
Name attachments clearly; files above 25 MB go as Drive links.
Reply to one person by default; use Reply all with care.
Archive, star and search keep a phone inbox manageable.

activity.title: Inbox workout
steps: Send yourself an email with a clear subject and one attached photo renamed sensibly.
Send a test email to two friends with one in To and one in Bcc, then ask whether each could see the other.
Archive ten old emails from your inbox and star one that needs action.
Use search with from: and has:attachment to find one old email with a file.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your sent test email and of a search using from: or has:attachment.

lessons.title: Writing clear, professional emails that get answered
objectives: Write a subject line that tells the reader what you need
Structure an email with greeting, purpose, details and closing
Choose the right tone for officials, customers and colleagues
Set up an email signature on your phone

blocks.text: A busy reader decides in seconds whether to open, answer or ignore your email. Clear emails get faster replies, make a good first impression on employers and customers, and leave a written record you can refer back to. The good news: a professional email follows a simple pattern that anyone can learn.

blocks.name: compose-email
blocks.alt: A person writing a new email
blocks.caption: A short, well-structured email is more likely to get a quick reply.

blocks.text: The five parts of a good email

items: **Subject line**: say what the email is about and what you need. "Request: Certificate copy for Amina Bello, Cohort 3" is better than "Hello" or a blank subject.
**Greeting**: "Dear Mrs Okafor," for someone senior or new to you; "Good morning Tunde," for a colleague you know. If you do not know the name, "Dear Admissions Team,".
**Purpose in the first line**: "I am writing to request a copy of my certificate." Do not make the reader search for your reason.
**Details**: short paragraphs or a short list with dates, reference numbers and what you have attached.
**Closing and name**: a clear next step, then "Kind regards," or "Thank you," and your full name and phone number.

blocks.title: How the reader meets your email
items: Sees sender and subject
Reads first line
Scans the details
Finds what to do
blocks.caption: Put the most important information where the reader looks first: the subject and the opening line.

blocks.title: Worked example: rewriting a weak email
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ilorin wants a shop owner to pay for 20 aprons she delivered. Her first draft, with no subject, reads: "hello sir pls I need my money the aprons I brought, you said you will pay."
steps: She adds a subject: "Invoice for 20 aprons delivered 12 May".
She opens with "Dear Mr Adeyemi," and states the purpose: "I am writing about payment for the 20 aprons delivered on 12 May."
She gives the details: "The agreed price was 4,500 naira each, a total of 90,000 naira. The invoice is attached."
She gives a clear next step: "Please make the transfer by Friday 23 May to the account on the invoice, or let me know if you need anything else."
She closes with "Kind regards, Rukayat Bello, Rukayat Aprons, 0803 000 0000 (example number)".
blocks.result: The new email is polite, specific and easy to act on, and gives Rukayat a dated written record of what was agreed.

blocks.text: Choosing the right tone

head: Reader
Tone
Opening example
rows: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to apply for...
Good afternoon Mrs Eze, thank you for your order...
Hi Tunde, quick update on Saturday's meeting...

items: Write in full sentences. Avoid text-message spelling like "pls", "u" and "tnx" in formal emails.
Do not write a whole email in CAPITAL LETTERS. It reads like shouting.
Keep it short: if the email is longer than your phone screen, think about what you can remove.
Mention every attachment in the body, so the reader knows to look for it.
Read it once before sending, out loud if possible. Check names, amounts and dates.

blocks.text: Add a signature once

A **signature** is text added automatically to the end of each email you send. In the Gmail app open Settings, tap your account, and choose **Mobile signature**. A useful signature has your full name, your role or business name and a phone number. Keep it to two or three lines.

blocks.title: Replying in good time
blocks.text: Try to answer work and customer emails within one working day. If you need more time, send a short reply: "Thank you, I have received this and will respond by Thursday." This keeps trust while you prepare a full answer.

blocks.title: Think before you send
blocks.text: Email can be forwarded and kept forever. Do not write anything in anger, and never put your BVN, card details, PIN or passwords in an email.

When you receive a long email thread, reply at the top and keep the earlier messages below. This lets everyone see the history. Change the subject only if the topic has truly changed, so the conversation stays easy to find later.
Email or WhatsApp?

Many Nigerian businesses run almost entirely on WhatsApp, and that is fine for quick questions. Email is better when you need a formal record: job applications, invoices, agreements about prices and dates, complaints to an organisation, and anything you may need to prove later. A good habit is to confirm important WhatsApp agreements in a short email: "Following our chat today, this confirms 20 aprons at 4,500 naira each, delivery on 12 May."

Applying for a job by email has its own rules. Put the job title and your name in the subject, write three or four short sentences in the body saying which job, why you fit and what is attached, and attach your CV as a PDF named with your full name. Do not send an empty email with only an attachment.

takeaways: The subject line and first sentence carry your main message.
Use greeting, purpose, details, next step and closing.
Match the tone to the reader and avoid text-message spelling.
Set a short mobile signature with your name and phone number.

activity.title: Write a real email
steps: Choose a real situation: a job enquiry, a customer follow-up or a request to an office.
Write the subject line first, then the five parts from this lesson.
Set up a mobile signature in Gmail settings.
Send the email to yourself first, read it on your phone, fix any mistakes, then send it to the real recipient or save it as a draft.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your finished email showing the subject line, structure and signature.

lessons.title: Spam, phishing emails and scam SMS
objectives: Explain spam, phishing, smishing and vishing in simple words
Spot the warning signs in a suspicious email or SMS
Check the real sender address behind a display name
Report and delete phishing messages in Gmail

blocks.text: **Spam** is unwanted bulk mail, mostly adverts. It is annoying but usually harmless. **Phishing** is different: a message that pretends to come from someone you trust, such as your bank, a delivery company, a network provider or even Google, to trick you into giving away a password, an OTP, card details or money. When it arrives by SMS it is often called **smishing**, and by phone call **vishing**.

blocks.name: data-thief
blocks.alt: A masked figure taking information from a screen
blocks.caption: Phishing tries to make you hand over your details yourself, so your judgement is the main defence.

blocks.text: The warning signs

items: **Urgency or fear**: "Your account will be blocked in 24 hours", "Your BVN has been suspended".
**A prize or money you did not expect**: lottery wins, grants, "you have been selected" for a loan or job.
**A request for secrets**: PIN, OTP, password, card number or BVN. Real banks do not ask for these by email, SMS or call.
**A link or attachment you were not expecting**, especially files ending in .apk, .exe or .zip.
**A sender address that does not match** the organisation, or a free Gmail or Yahoo address claiming to be a bank.
**A generic greeting** like "Dear Customer" and spelling or grammar mistakes.

blocks.text: Check who really sent it

In Gmail, the bold name you see is only a **display name**, and anyone can type any name. Tap the sender's name or the small arrow under it to see the real address. "Zenith Bank Security" sending from zenith-alerts-verify@gmail.com is a scam. Then apply what you learned in Module 1: check the domain in any link by pressing and holding it, without opening it.

blocks.title: Suspicious message routine
items: Pause, do not tap
Check sender address
Contact official channel
Report as phishing
Delete
blocks.caption: Slowing down and checking through a channel you already trust defeats most phishing.

blocks.title: Worked example: a fake delivery SMS
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Abuja is expecting a parcel. She receives an SMS: "Your package is held at our warehouse. Pay 1,250 naira customs fee here to release it" with a link.
steps: She pauses, because the message does not name the shop or the tracking number she was given.
She presses and holds the link and sees a strange domain unrelated to the courier.
She opens the order confirmation email from the shop she bought from and uses the tracking link there instead.
The tracking page shows the parcel is out for delivery with no fee due.
She deletes the SMS and tells her mother, who orders online often, about the trick.
blocks.result: Esther saved 1,250 naira and, more importantly, did not type her card details into a fake payment page.

blocks.text: Report and clean up in Gmail

items: Open the suspicious email. Do not tap links, open attachments or reply.
Tap the three dots at the top right. Choose Report spam. On the web version you can also choose Report phishing.
If you see a yellow or red warning banner from Gmail at the top of an email, trust it.
If a real contact's account sends you a strange link, call them on the phone to warn them their account may be hacked.

blocks.title: If you already clicked or typed
blocks.text: Act at once. If you entered a password, change it from the official app or website and turn on two-step verification. If you shared bank details, a card number or an OTP, call your bank's official number from the back of your card immediately and ask them to block the card or account. Speed matters more than embarrassment.

blocks.title: Phone calls too
blocks.text: A caller who says they are from your bank and asks you to "confirm" an OTP that just arrived is a fraudster, even if they already know your name and part of your account number. Hang up and call the number on your card.

Scammers also reach people through WhatsApp and Facebook, pretending to be friends whose accounts they have taken over, asking for urgent transfers. The same routine works everywhere: pause, verify through another channel such as a phone call, and never send money or codes because of a message alone.
Common phishing stories in Nigeria

head: The story
What they want
The safe response
rows: Your BVN or NIN must be updated or your account will be frozen
Visit your bank app or branch yourself; never use the link
You won a promo from a network or bank
A "processing fee" or your card details
Real promos never ask winners to pay first
Free data or a government grant, share with ten groups
Check the official website of the named body; do not forward
Your package is held, pay a small fee
Card details on a fake page
Use the tracking link from the shop's own email or app
A friend's WhatsApp asks for an urgent transfer
Call the friend on a normal phone call first

blocks.text: Notice that every story ends with you doing something quickly: tapping, paying, sharing or reading out a code. That speed is the scammer's tool. Your tool is a short pause and a check through a channel you already trust.

takeaways: Phishing pretends to be someone you trust to steal codes, passwords or money.
Urgency, prizes and requests for PIN, OTP or BVN are red flags.
Tap the display name to see the real sender address.
Report phishing, and contact your bank at once if you shared anything.

activity.title: Phishing hunt
steps: Open your Gmail Spam folder and your SMS inbox and find two suspicious messages.
For each one, list the warning signs from this lesson that you can see.
Tap the sender name in a suspicious email and write down the real address.
Report one email as spam or phishing and delete the suspicious SMS.
activity.evidence: A note listing the two messages (with personal details hidden) and the warning signs you found in each.

quiz.q: Tolu is emailing a price list to 40 customers who do not know each other. Where should she put their addresses?
options: In To
In Cc
In Bcc
In the subject line
quiz.explain: Bcc hides each customer's address from the others and prevents mass reply-all.

quiz.q: Which subject line is most professional for a certificate request?
options: Hello
Pls urgent!!!
Request: Certificate copy for Amina Bello, Cohort 3
(no subject)
quiz.explain: A good subject says what the email is about and what you need.

quiz.q: An email says it is from "GTBank Support". What should you check first?
options: The colour of the logo
The real sender address behind the display name
How long the email is
Whether it has a nice greeting
quiz.explain: Anyone can type any display name. The real address reveals who sent it.

quiz.q: Ada clicked a link in an SMS and typed her card number into a payment page before realising it was fake. What should she do next?
options: Wait to see if money goes missing
Reply to the SMS asking for a refund
Call her bank on the number on the back of her card immediately
Delete the SMS and forget it
quiz.explain: Fast action through the bank's official number can block the card before money is taken.

quiz.q: What does Archive do in Gmail?
options: Deletes the email forever
Moves the email out of the inbox but keeps it searchable in All mail
Sends the email to spam
Forwards it to your recovery email
quiz.explain: Archived mail is kept and can be found with search; it just leaves the inbox.

quiz.q: Why should you add a recovery phone and recovery email to your Google account?
options: To receive more adverts
So Google can confirm it is you if you forget the password or lose your phone
To make the account load faster
Because Gmail will not send emails without them
quiz.explain: Recovery details are your spare key for getting back into your account.

modules.title: Protecting your accounts, connection and privacy
modules.overview: Lock your accounts with strong passwords, a password manager and passkeys, then add two-step verification so a stolen password is not enough. Learn to use Wi-Fi safely and to set the privacy controls on your phone, Google account, WhatsApp and Facebook.

lessons.title: Strong passwords, password managers and passkeys
objectives: Create a long passphrase that is strong and easy to remember
Explain why reusing one password across accounts is dangerous
Save and check passwords with Google Password Manager
Set up a passkey for your Google account

blocks.text: Your password is the main lock on your email, WhatsApp backups, social media and sometimes your money. Criminals do not usually guess passwords one by one. They use computer programs that try millions of common passwords, and lists of passwords leaked from websites that were hacked. A good password beats both.

blocks.name: secure-password
blocks.alt: A large padlock beside a password field
blocks.caption: Length and uniqueness, not clever symbols, are what make a password strong.

blocks.text: What makes a password weak

items: **Personal details**: your name, child's name, birthday, phone number or year, such as Chioma1990. These are easy to find on social media.
**Common patterns**: 123456, password, qwerty, 112233 or your name followed by 123.
**Short length**: anything under 12 characters can be cracked much faster.
**Reuse**: the same password on many sites. If one small website leaks it, criminals try it on your Gmail, Facebook and bank.

blocks.text: The passphrase method

Pick **four random words** that do not belong together, then join them with a number or symbol. For example: **Mango-Bicycle-Rain-Okra7**. It is long, easy to picture and hard for programs to guess. Do not use a famous saying or song line, because those are in criminals' word lists. Use a different passphrase for each important account.

blocks.title: Weak versus strong
items: Weak password
Strong passphrase
blocks.caption: A long, unique passphrase protects you even if another website is hacked.

blocks.text: Let a password manager remember for you

Nobody can remember twenty different strong passwords. A **password manager** stores them securely and fills them in for you. Android phones and Chrome include **Google Password Manager**, linked to your Google account. When you create an account in Chrome, it can suggest a strong random password and save it. You can view saved passwords at **passwords.google.com** after confirming it is you.

Google Password Manager also has a **Password Checkup** that warns you if any saved password has appeared in a known data leak, is weak, or is reused. Run it and change any password it flags, starting with email and banking. This works only if your Google account itself is very well protected, which is why the next lesson on two-step verification matters.
Passkeys: signing in without a password

A **passkey** lets you sign in with the same fingerprint, face scan or screen lock PIN you use to unlock your phone. Your phone keeps a secret key that never leaves the device and only works on the real website or app it was made for. That means a fake website cannot trick you into handing it over, which makes passkeys strong protection against phishing. Google, WhatsApp and many other services now support them.

items: Make sure your phone has a screen lock (PIN, pattern, fingerprint or face).
Open myaccount.google.com and tap Security.
Find Passkeys and security keys under How you sign in to Google, and tap Create a passkey.
Confirm with your fingerprint or screen lock. Next time you sign in on a new device, Google can ask your phone to confirm instead of asking for a password.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixing reused passwords
blocks.context: For example, Yetunde in Lagos used the password Yetty1988 for Gmail, Facebook, Jumia and a recipe website. The recipe website was hacked, and she later got a Gmail alert about a sign-in attempt from another country.
steps: She changes her Gmail password first to a new passphrase: Kettle-Lagoon-Pepper-Drum4.
She opens passwords.google.com and runs Password Checkup, which shows the old password reused on four sites and found in a leak.
She changes Facebook and Jumia next, using Chrome's suggested strong passwords and saving them in the manager.
She creates a passkey for her Google account so she can sign in with her fingerprint.
blocks.result: Each account now has its own password, and the leaked one no longer opens anything.

blocks.title: Never share it
blocks.text: No genuine bank, network, employer or WODDI staff member will ask for your password or a sign-in code. If someone asks, it is a scam, however official they sound.

You can check whether your email address has appeared in a known data breach at **haveibeenpwned.com**, a free service run by a respected security researcher. If it has, change the password for that site and anywhere you reused it.
If you prefer paper

Writing passwords in a notebook kept safely at home is far better than reusing one weak password everywhere. Keep the notebook out of your handbag and away from visitors, never photograph it, and do not label it "passwords". Your phone's screen lock PIN is also a password: use at least six digits and never your birth year.

takeaways: Length and uniqueness matter more than strange symbols.
Four random words make a strong, memorable passphrase.
Google Password Manager saves passwords and warns about leaked or reused ones.
Passkeys use your fingerprint or screen lock and resist phishing.

activity.title: Password clean-up
steps: Write a list of your five most important accounts, starting with email and banking.
Create a new four-word passphrase for your email and change it.
Open passwords.google.com and run Password Checkup.
Change any password it marks as compromised or reused.
Create a passkey for your Google account.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of Password Checkup after your changes (with no passwords visible) and a note of which accounts you updated.

lessons.title: Two-step verification for Gmail, WhatsApp and Facebook
objectives: Explain how two-step verification stops someone who has your password
Turn on 2-Step Verification for your Google account
Set a two-step verification PIN in WhatsApp
Save backup codes so you are never locked out

blocks.text: **Two-step verification** (also called 2SV or two-factor authentication, 2FA) means signing in needs two things: something you **know**, such as your password, and something you **have**, such as your phone. If a criminal steals your password through phishing or a data leak, they still cannot get in without the second step.

blocks.name: fingerprint-login
blocks.alt: A person confirming a login with a fingerprint on a phone
blocks.caption: The second step proves you have your own phone, not just your password.

blocks.text: Kinds of second step

head: Method
How it works
Strength
rows: Your phone shows "Is it you trying to sign in?" and you tap Yes
An app such as Google Authenticator shows a 6-digit code that changes every 30 seconds
A code is sent to your phone number
Better than nothing, but weaker because of SIM-swap fraud
One-time codes you print or write down for emergencies
Your safety net if you lose the phone
Fingerprint or screen lock on your phone

blocks.title: Signing in with 2SV
items: Enter password
Google asks your phone
You tap Yes
Signed in
blocks.caption: Without your phone in hand, a thief with your password stops at step two.

blocks.text: Turn it on for Google

items: Open myaccount.google.com and tap Security.
Under How you sign in to Google, tap 2-Step Verification and follow the prompts.
Add at least two second steps, for example Google prompts on your phone and an authenticator app, plus your phone number as a fallback.
Tap Backup codes and get your codes. Write them on paper and keep them somewhere safe at home, not in a photo on the same phone.

blocks.text: Turn it on for WhatsApp

WhatsApp accounts are often stolen when someone tricks you into reading out the 6-digit SMS code WhatsApp sends when an account is registered on a new phone. A **two-step verification PIN** blocks this: even with that SMS code, the thief also needs your PIN.

items: In WhatsApp, open Settings, then Account, then Two-step verification.
Tap Turn on and create a 6-digit PIN that is not your birthday or bank PIN.
Add an email address so you can reset the PIN if you forget it.
WhatsApp will ask for the PIN from time to time to help you remember it.

blocks.title: The "wrong code" trick
blocks.text: A message from a friend's number says: "I sent you a code by mistake, please send it back to me." That code is your own WhatsApp registration code, and sending it hands over your account. Never share any code that arrives on your phone.
Facebook, Instagram and banks

On Facebook and Instagram, open Accounts Center, then Password and security, then Two-factor authentication, and choose an authentication app or SMS. Nigerian bank apps use their own second steps, such as a transaction PIN, a one-time code by SMS or email, a hardware token, or a code generator inside the app. Set these up through your bank's official app or branch, and never share the codes.

blocks.title: Worked example: a stolen password that failed
blocks.context: For example, Patience in Benin City typed her Gmail password into a fake login page by mistake. She had turned on 2-Step Verification with Google prompts a month earlier.
steps: Minutes later her phone shows: "Is it you trying to sign in? Device: Windows, location: another country."
She taps No, it's not me. Google blocks the sign-in.
Google guides her to change her password, and she uses a new passphrase.
She opens Security Checkup and signs out of any devices she does not recognise.
blocks.result: The thief had her correct password but could not get in, because the second step was on Patience's phone.

blocks.title: Changing phones
blocks.text: Before you sell, give away or reset a phone, make sure your authenticator codes and Google prompts are moved to the new phone, and keep your backup codes handy. Google Authenticator can sync codes to your Google account so they are not lost with the phone.

Start with your email, because email is used to reset almost every other account. Then do WhatsApp, Facebook and your bank. It takes about ten minutes per account and is one of the most effective things you can do for your safety online.

Two-step verification sometimes feels like an extra hurdle, but you only meet it on new devices or unusual sign-ins. On your own phone, you rarely notice it. If you are helping an older relative, set up Google prompts for them, because tapping Yes or No is easier than typing codes.

If you ever get a sign-in prompt or code that you did not ask for, it means someone has your password. Tap No or ignore the code, then change your password straight away. Do not approve a prompt just to make it go away.

takeaways: 2SV needs something you know and something you have.
Google prompts, authenticator apps and passkeys are stronger than SMS codes.
A WhatsApp two-step PIN stops account theft through a stolen SMS code.
Keep backup codes on paper and never share any code sent to your phone.

activity.title: Lock the doors
steps: Turn on 2-Step Verification for your Google account with Google prompts.
Download and write down your Google backup codes, and store the paper safely.
Turn on WhatsApp two-step verification with a 6-digit PIN and recovery email.
Turn on two-factor authentication for Facebook or Instagram if you use them.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of the 2-Step Verification "On" page in Google and the Two-step verification screen in WhatsApp.

lessons.title: Using Wi-Fi and hotspots safely
objectives: Explain the risks of free public Wi-Fi
Decide which tasks are safe on public Wi-Fi and which are not
Secure a home router, MiFi or phone hotspot with a strong password
Remove saved Wi-Fi networks and turn off automatic connection

blocks.text: Wi-Fi saves your data bundle, which makes free Wi-Fi at hotels, eateries, airports, malls and event venues very attractive. The risk is that you do not control the network. Anyone can create a Wi-Fi network and give it a trusted-sounding name such as "Hotel Guest Free" or "Airport WiFi". Whoever runs the network can see which websites you visit and may try to show you fake login pages.

blocks.name: internet-on-the-go
blocks.alt: A woman using her phone while travelling
blocks.caption: Public Wi-Fi is handy on the go, but it belongs to someone else.

blocks.text: What public Wi-Fi exposes

items: **Fake networks**: a criminal sets up a network with the same name as the real one, so your phone joins the wrong one.
**Snooping**: on websites without HTTPS, people on the same network can read what you send.
**Fake login pages**: a "sign in to use Wi-Fi" page that asks for your Google or Facebook password.
**Shared networks**: other devices on the same Wi-Fi can try to connect to your phone if sharing features are left on.

blocks.text: HTTPS, which you met in Module 1, now protects most websites and apps, so public Wi-Fi is much safer than it used to be. Still, a fake network can trick you, and you cannot always tell. The safe habit is simple: **use public Wi-Fi for low-risk things, and switch to mobile data for anything involving money or passwords**.

blocks.title: Is this task safe on public Wi-Fi?
items: Reading news: fine
Watching course videos: fine
Logging into email: use data
Banking and payments: use data
axes: Need to type passwords or pay
blocks.caption: The more a task involves passwords or money, the more you should switch from public Wi-Fi to mobile data.

blocks.text: Safe habits on public Wi-Fi

items: Ask staff for the exact network name and password, and check it matches before you join.
Never type your email, bank or social media password into a Wi-Fi sign-in page. A genuine venue page asks only for a code, phone number or room number.
Do banking, transfers and shopping on mobile data, not public Wi-Fi.
If Chrome shows "Not secure" or a certificate warning, close the page.
When you leave, go to Settings, Wi-Fi, tap the network and choose Forget, so your phone does not reconnect automatically.

blocks.title: Stop automatic joining
blocks.text: In your Wi-Fi settings, turn off options like "Connect to public networks" or "Auto reconnect" for networks you do not own. Your phone will then only join networks you choose each time.
Securing your own Wi-Fi, MiFi or hotspot

Many families and small businesses share internet through a home router, a portable MiFi device or a phone's **personal hotspot**. If it has a weak or no password, neighbours can use your data and may see your devices. Protect it like this:

items: Set the security type to **WPA2** or **WPA3** (never "Open" or the old WEP).
Use a long Wi-Fi password, for example a four-word passphrase.
Change the default admin password printed on the router or MiFi sticker. The admin page address is usually printed on the sticker too.
Change the network name to something that does not include your name, house number or business.
Turn off your phone hotspot when you are not using it, and check the list of connected devices for strangers.

blocks.title: Worked example: the eatery Wi-Fi
blocks.context: For example, Zainab is waiting for a client at an eatery in Kano. Her phone shows two networks, "Eatery_Free_WiFi" and "Eatery Free WiFi", and her client is about to pay her 45,000 naira by transfer.
steps: She asks the cashier, who says the real network has no underscores and gives her the password.
She joins that network to download a course video for later, which uses no personal details.
When she needs to check whether the 45,000 naira has arrived, she turns Wi-Fi off and opens her bank app on mobile data.
Before leaving, she taps the network in Settings and chooses Forget.
blocks.result: Zainab saved data on the large download and kept her banking off a network she did not control.

blocks.title: What about VPN apps?
blocks.text: A VPN encrypts your traffic between your phone and the VPN company, which can help on public Wi-Fi. But many free VPN apps collect and sell data or show heavy adverts. If you use one, choose a well-known paid provider and remember that the VPN company can see your traffic instead.

Keep your phone's software updated through Settings, System update or Software update, ideally over Wi-Fi you trust. Updates close security holes that criminals use on shared networks. Also turn off Bluetooth and file-sharing features when you are not using them.

Be careful with public USB charging points in malls and airports too. Use your own charger plugged into a wall socket, or a power bank. If your phone asks whether to allow file transfer or "trust this device" when you plug into a public port, choose charging only.

takeaways: Anyone can create a Wi-Fi network with a trusted-sounding name.
Use public Wi-Fi for low-risk browsing; use mobile data for money and passwords.
Never enter account passwords on a Wi-Fi sign-in page.
Secure your own router, MiFi or hotspot with WPA2 or WPA3 and a long password.

activity.title: Wi-Fi safety check
steps: Open Settings, then Wi-Fi, and view your saved networks. Forget any public networks you no longer use.
Turn off automatic connection to open or public networks.
Open your personal hotspot settings and set a long password with WPA2 or WPA3 security.
If you have a home router or MiFi, check that its admin password is no longer the default on the sticker.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your hotspot settings (password hidden) and a note listing the saved networks you removed.

lessons.title: Privacy settings on your phone, Google account, WhatsApp and Facebook
objectives: Review and remove app permissions such as location, camera and contacts
Run Google Privacy Checkup and Security Checkup
Set WhatsApp and Facebook privacy so strangers see less
Decide what is unsafe to post publicly

blocks.text: **Privacy** means you decide who sees information about you: your phone number, location, photos, family details and what you search for. Criminals use these details to build convincing scams. For example, a fraudster who knows your child's school from a photo of the uniform can pretend to be a teacher calling about an emergency.

blocks.name: private-data
blocks.alt: A person protecting a folder of personal data with a lock
blocks.caption: A few minutes in your settings decides who can see your personal information.

blocks.text: 1. Phone permissions

Apps ask for **permissions** to use parts of your phone, such as location, camera, microphone, contacts and files. A torch app does not need your contacts; a game does not need your location. On Android open Settings and search for **Permission manager**. Tap a permission such as Location to see which apps have it, and change any that do not need it to **Don't allow** or **Allow only while using the app**.

blocks.title: Find your phone
blocks.text: Make sure Find My Device is turned on (search for it in Settings). If your phone is lost or stolen, you can sign in at android.com/find from another device to ring it, lock it or erase it. A screen lock PIN or fingerprint is essential for this to protect you.
2. Your Google account

items: Open myaccount.google.com and tap Data and privacy, then Privacy Checkup, or go straight to myaccount.google.com/privacycheckup.
Review Web and App Activity, Location History (Timeline) and YouTube History. Choose whether to keep them, turn them off or set auto-delete after a few months.
Check what personal information others can see on your Google profile.
Then open Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup and remove any devices or third-party apps you do not recognise.

blocks.text: 3. WhatsApp

Open WhatsApp, then Settings, then **Privacy**. Set Last seen and online, Profile photo, About and Status to **My contacts**. Under **Groups**, choose My contacts so strangers cannot add you to scam investment or loan groups. Under **Calls**, turn on Silence unknown callers to stop spam calls ringing. Use **Privacy checkup** at the top of the Privacy screen for a guided walk-through.
4. Facebook and other social media

In Facebook, open Settings and use **Privacy Checkup**. Set who can see your future posts to Friends, limit who can see your friends list, phone number and email, and review who can look you up using your phone number. Do the same review for Instagram and TikTok if you use them, including whether your account is public or private.

blocks.title: Monthly privacy check
items: App permissions reviewed
Google Privacy Checkup done
WhatsApp set to My contacts
Facebook posts set to Friends
Find My Device on
blocks.caption: Repeat these five checks once a month, and after installing new apps.

blocks.text: What not to post publicly

head: Do not post
Why
rows: Photos of your BVN slip, NIN slip, ID card, ATM card or cheque
Numbers can be used for fraud and identity theft
Your child's school name or uniform, with their full name
Travel plans or "we are away" posts while away
Boarding passes and tickets with barcodes
Your home address and daily routine
Makes you easy to locate and follow

blocks.title: Worked example: a privacy tidy-up
blocks.context: For example, Aisha in Abuja sells shoes on WhatsApp and noticed strangers adding her to "forex investment" groups and calling at night.
steps: She sets WhatsApp Groups to My contacts and turns on Silence unknown callers.
She moves customer chats to a separate WhatsApp Business number, so her personal profile photo stays visible only to contacts.
In Permission manager she finds a photo-editing app with access to her contacts and location, and removes both.
She runs Google Privacy Checkup and sets location history to auto-delete after three months.
blocks.result: The scam group invitations and night calls stop, and fewer apps can see where she is or who she knows.

blocks.title: Your rights in Nigeria
blocks.text: The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 gives people rights over their personal data, including the right to know how it is used. It is enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). Organisations that collect your data should explain why and protect it.

Privacy is not about hiding; it is about choosing. A business page can be public while your family photos stay private. Before you post, ask: would I be comfortable if a stranger who wanted to cheat me saw this?

Be just as careful with other people's privacy. Ask before posting photos of friends or their children, remove phone numbers before forwarding screenshots, and do not share personal details of customers outside the reason they gave them to you. In a business, collect only the customer information you really need.

takeaways: Remove app permissions that an app does not need for its job.
Google Privacy Checkup and Security Checkup show what is collected and who has access.
Set WhatsApp profile, groups and calls to My contacts and silence unknown callers.
Never post ID slips, cards, travel plans or your child's school details publicly.

activity.title: Privacy tune-up
steps: Open Permission manager and remove Location or Contacts from at least two apps that do not need them.
Run Google Privacy Checkup and set auto-delete for your activity.
Set WhatsApp Last seen, Profile photo and Groups to My contacts, and turn on Silence unknown callers.
Run Facebook Privacy Checkup if you use Facebook.
Confirm Find My Device is on.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your WhatsApp Privacy screen and Google Privacy Checkup, plus a note of which app permissions you removed.

quiz.q: Which password is strongest?
options: Chioma1990
Mango-Bicycle-Rain-Okra7
P@ssw0rd
quiz.explain: Four random words make a long passphrase that is hard to guess and not based on personal details.

quiz.q: Emeka's password was leaked from a shopping site. He used the same password for Gmail. What protects his Gmail best right now?
options: Nothing, because the password is known
2-Step Verification on his Google account, plus changing the password
Logging out of the shopping site
Clearing his browser history
quiz.explain: With 2SV the thief also needs his phone, and changing the password closes the leak.

quiz.q: A friend's WhatsApp sends: "I sent you a 6-digit code by mistake, please forward it." What is happening?
options: A normal mistake, so forward it
Someone is trying to take over your WhatsApp account with your registration code
WhatsApp is updating
Your friend needs data
quiz.explain: That code registers your WhatsApp on another phone. Never share codes; set a two-step PIN.

quiz.q: Zainab is on free eatery Wi-Fi and needs to check a bank transfer. What should she do?
options: Use the eatery Wi-Fi, since it has a password
Turn off Wi-Fi and use her bank app on mobile data
Open the bank website in Incognito on the Wi-Fi
Ask the cashier to check for her
quiz.explain: Money and passwords belong on mobile data, not a network she does not control.

quiz.q: Why are passkeys strong protection against phishing?
options: They are very long passwords you type
They only work on the real website or app and never leave your phone
They are sent by SMS
They change your phone number
quiz.explain: A fake website cannot receive a passkey, because the key only works with the genuine site.

quiz.q: Where on Android can you see which apps have access to your location?
options: In the Play Store reviews
In Permission manager in Settings
In WhatsApp Status
In the phone dialler
quiz.explain: Permission manager lists apps by permission so you can remove access they do not need.

modules.title: Apps, money and everyday online tools
modules.overview: Install apps safely from the Play Store, protect your money from SIM-swap and banking scams, store and share files in Google Drive, and join video calls and online classes with confidence. This module turns your safety skills into everyday habits.

lessons.title: Downloading apps safely from the Play Store
objectives: Check an app's developer, reviews and Data safety section before installing
