Explain why APK files from WhatsApp or websites are risky
Run Google Play Protect and review app permissions
Recognise fake loan and investment apps

blocks.text: On Android phones, the **Google Play Store** is the official place to get apps. Google checks apps before and after they are published, and a built-in tool called **Google Play Protect** scans the apps on your phone for harmful behaviour. Fake and harmful apps still sometimes get into the Play Store, so you need to look before you tap Install.

blocks.name: app-installation
blocks.alt: A phone installing a new app
blocks.caption: A minute of checking before Install can save you from a fake or harmful app.

blocks.text: Five checks before you install

items: **Developer name**: under the app name, tap the developer. A real bank app is published by the bank itself, for example the bank's full name, not a person or an unknown company. Open the bank's official website and use its Play Store link if unsure.

**Downloads and reviews**: real popular apps have many downloads and many reviews. Read the most recent reviews, not just the stars. Many reviews complaining about stolen money or harassment are a clear warning.
**Data safety**: scroll to the Data safety section to see what the app collects and shares, such as location, contacts or photos.
**Permissions that make sense**: a calculator does not need your contacts. A loan app that wants your contacts and photos may use them to shame you to your family.
**Name and logo copies**: scammers copy famous apps with slightly different names or logos. Compare carefully.

blocks.title: Before you tap Install
items: Developer is the real organisation
Many downloads, honest recent reviews
Data safety looks reasonable
Permissions fit the purpose
Name and logo exact
blocks.caption: If any check fails, do not install the app.

blocks.text: Why you should avoid APK files

An **APK** is an Android app file. People send APKs on WhatsApp or websites offer them for "free premium" versions of paid apps, cheaper data apps or "investment" platforms. These files skip the Play Store checks and are a common way to install software that reads your SMS (including bank OTPs), shows fake login screens or steals contacts. Android blocks them unless you switch on **Install unknown apps** for a particular app such as Chrome or WhatsApp. Keep that setting off.

blocks.title: Fake loan apps
blocks.text: Some loan apps charge very high hidden fees and harass borrowers by messaging their contacts. In Nigeria, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) publishes a list of digital lenders it has approved. Check that list on the FCCPC's official website before you borrow through any app, and never give a loan app access to your contacts or photos.
Use Play Protect and keep apps tidy

items: Open Play Store, tap your profile picture, then **Play Protect**. Make sure scanning is on and tap Scan.
Update apps regularly; updates fix security problems. Use Wi-Fi to save data, as you set up in Module 1.
Uninstall apps you no longer use. Each unused app is one more thing that can collect data or be hacked.
If an app suddenly shows adverts over other apps, drains your battery or data, or you cannot find its icon, uninstall it in Settings, Apps.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing the real bank app
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Owerri wants to install her bank's app. Searching the Play Store shows three apps with the bank's logo.
steps: The first has 10 million plus downloads and the developer is the bank's full registered name.
The second is called the bank name plus "Loan Plus", developed by an unknown company, with recent reviews saying it took money.
The third has under 1,000 downloads and asks for SMS and contacts permission.
She opens the bank's official website in Chrome, taps its Google Play link, and it opens the first app. She installs it.
She reports the other two apps using the three-dot menu and Flag as inappropriate.
blocks.result: Ngozi installed the genuine app and helped warn others about the copies.

blocks.title: On iPhone
blocks.text: iPhones install apps only from Apple's App Store. The same checks apply: developer name, reviews, privacy details (called App Privacy) and permissions.

Be careful with "earn money" apps that pay you to watch adverts, complete tasks or invite friends, and "investment" apps promising fixed high returns every day. Many collapse and disappear with members' money. Real investments explain the risk and are registered with the relevant regulator, such as the Securities and Exchange Commission in Nigeria.

Remember that installing an app is only the start. After installing, open your phone's Settings, Apps, choose the new app and look at Permissions again. Turn off anything that is not needed for what you use the app for.

If a harmful app has already been installed, act quickly: uninstall it, run a Play Protect scan, change the passwords of any accounts you used while it was on the phone, and tell your bank if it could read your SMS. If the phone still behaves strangely, back up your photos and documents and ask a trusted technician to reset it.

takeaways: Install apps only from the Play Store (or App Store), and check the developer.
Read recent reviews and the Data safety section before installing.
Keep Install unknown apps off and never install APKs from chats.
Run Play Protect and remove apps you do not use.

activity.title: App audit
steps: Run a Play Protect scan from the Play Store.
List every app on your phone and uninstall at least three you no longer use.
For one financial app you use, check the developer name and Data safety section.
Search Settings for Install unknown apps and make sure it is off for Chrome, WhatsApp and your file manager.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of the Play Protect result and a list of the apps you removed.

lessons.title: Mobile money and SIM-swap scams: keeping your money safe
objectives: Explain how a SIM-swap scam lets criminals receive your bank codes
Recognise the warning signs that your SIM may have been swapped
Set up bank and mobile money apps with strong protection
Follow an emergency plan if money is taken or your SIM stops working

blocks.text: Many Nigerian women now receive and send money through bank apps, USSD codes and fintech apps such as OPay, Moniepoint and PalmPay. These tools are convenient and generally safe when used carefully. Most money lost online is not lost because criminals broke the bank's systems, but because they tricked someone into sharing a code or took control of their phone number.

blocks.name: mobile-pay
blocks.alt: A woman making a payment on her phone
blocks.caption: Your phone number and your codes are the keys to your money.

blocks.text: How a SIM-swap scam works

Your bank sends one-time passwords (**OTPs**) and alerts to your phone number. In a **SIM swap**, a criminal convinces or bribes someone at a network outlet to move your number onto a new SIM card in their possession, often using details they gathered from phishing or social media. Your own SIM stops working. Now the criminal receives your OTPs and can reset passwords or approve transfers.

blocks.title: A SIM-swap attack
items: Details stolen by phishing
Fake SIM replacement request
Your SIM loses service
Criminal receives your OTPs
Money moved out
blocks.caption: The attack is fastest in the first hours after your SIM goes dead, so speed is your defence.

blocks.text: Warning signs

items: Your phone suddenly shows **No service** or **SIM not registered** for a long time while people around you on the same network have signal.
You get an SMS saying your SIM replacement request has been processed when you made none.
You stop receiving calls and SMS, while friends say your phone rings or goes to voicemail.
You get bank emails about sign-ins or transfers you did not make.

blocks.text: Emergency plan: act within minutes

items: Borrow another phone and call your network's customer care to report a possible SIM swap and ask them to block the number.

Call your bank's official number (from the back of your card or saved in advance) and ask them to freeze your account and cards. Many Nigerian banks have a short emergency USSD code to block your account; find yours on the bank's official website today and save it.
Change your email password and check your email's 2-Step Verification, because email is used to reset bank logins.
Visit your network's office with your ID to recover your number, and your bank to report the fraud in writing.
Keep a record of times, calls and reference numbers for any complaint.

blocks.title: Prepare before it happens
blocks.text: Today, save your bank's fraud line and emergency block code in your phone contacts and also write them on paper at home. During a SIM swap your phone may not work, and you will need the numbers to call from another phone.
Protect your money apps

head: Do
Do not
rows: Use a transaction PIN different from your phone lock and ATM PIN
Turn on fingerprint login in the bank app
Let others use your phone with the bank app open
Set daily transfer limits that match your real needs
Keep the highest limit if you never send that much
Read every debit alert and check your balance often
Ignore alerts you do not understand
Check the account name shown before confirming a transfer
Rush a transfer because someone is pressuring you

blocks.title: Worked example: the fake alert and the refund trick
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa sells foodstuff in Jos. A buyer says he has sent 38,000 naira for two bags of rice and shows her a screenshot of a transfer. Then he says he sent 83,000 by mistake and asks her to refund 45,000.
steps: Hauwa does not trust the screenshot or SMS. She opens her bank app and checks her real balance.
The balance shows no money arrived at all; the screenshot and SMS were fake.
She refuses to release the rice or send any refund until money shows in her app.
She warns the other traders in her market WhatsApp group about the trick.
blocks.result: Hauwa lost nothing, because she trusted only the balance inside her own bank app, not screenshots or SMS.

blocks.title: Codes are for you alone
blocks.text: Your PIN, OTP, password and BVN should never be told to anyone, including callers who say they are bank staff, network staff, or officials. Banks repeatedly warn customers that they will never ask for these. Anyone who asks is a fraudster.

Where your bank or email allows it, use an authenticator app, Google prompts or a passkey instead of SMS codes for signing in, as you learned in Module 3. This means a stolen phone number alone is not enough to break in. Also avoid posting your phone number together with your full name, date of birth and bank name online, since these details help criminals impersonate you at a network outlet.

Another costly mistake is sending money to the wrong account number. Always read the account name your app shows before you confirm. If money goes to the wrong person, contact your bank at once with the transaction details and ask them to start a recall; it is not guaranteed, but early reports have the best chance.

takeaways: A SIM swap moves your number to a criminal's SIM so they receive your OTPs.
Sudden No service while others have signal is a warning sign: act at once.
Call your network and bank from another phone; save emergency numbers in advance.
Trust only your bank app balance, never screenshots or SMS alerts alone.

activity.title: Money safety kit
steps: Find your bank's official fraud line and emergency block USSD code on its official website.
Save both in your contacts and write them on paper at home.
Check your bank app's transfer limit and lower it if it is higher than you need.
Turn on fingerprint login and set a transaction PIN that is different from your other PINs.
Write your own five-step SIM-swap emergency plan.
activity.evidence: Your written emergency card with the bank and network numbers (no PINs or account numbers), and a screenshot of your transfer limit setting.

lessons.title: Google Drive: storing, backing up and sharing files safely
objectives: Upload, organise and find files in Google Drive
Share a file with the right access: Viewer, Commenter or Editor
Scan paper documents into PDFs with your phone
Back up your phone's photos and WhatsApp chats

blocks.text: **Google Drive** is online storage that comes free with your Google account. Files you put in Drive are kept on Google's servers, so you can open them from any phone or computer by signing in. If your phone is lost, stolen or damaged, your files in Drive are still safe. Your free account has 15 GB of storage shared between Drive, Gmail and Google Photos.

blocks.name: cloud-files
blocks.caption: Files in Drive live online, so a lost phone does not mean lost documents.

blocks.text: Upload and organise

items: Install the Google Drive app from the Play Store if it is not already on your phone, and sign in with your Google account.
Tap the plus (+) button, then Upload, and choose a file or photo from your phone.
Tap plus, then Folder, to create folders such as Certificates, Business receipts and Children's school.
Press and hold a file, then choose Move to put it in a folder.
Use the search bar at the top to find files by name or even by words inside a document.

blocks.text: Scan paper into a PDF

Tap the plus button and choose **Scan**. Point the camera at a document such as a certificate, receipt or ID card, and Drive crops and straightens it into a clean PDF. Rename it clearly, for example **Certificate_Tailoring_2026.pdf**, and save it to the right folder. This is very useful for job and course applications that ask for uploaded documents.
Sharing with the right access

head: Access level
They can
Use it for
rows: Price lists, certificates you send to an employer
Read and add comments, but not change the file
Asking someone to review your CV
Change, delete and share the file
Only trusted team members working on the same file

blocks.text: To share, press and hold a file and choose **Share** to add a person's email, or **Manage access** to create a link. Under General access, **Restricted** means only people you add can open it. **Anyone with the link** means anyone who gets the link, even by forwarding, can open it. Use Restricted for personal documents.

blocks.title: How much access to give
items: Editor: very few
Commenter: reviewers
Viewer: most people
blocks.caption: Give the smallest level of access that lets the person do what they need.

blocks.title: Sensitive documents
blocks.text: Never set ID cards, BVN or NIN slips, bank statements or medical papers to Anyone with the link. Share them only with named people, and remove access when they no longer need it.
Back up photos and WhatsApp

items: **Photos**: in the Google Photos app, tap your profile picture and turn on Backup. Set it to back up only on Wi-Fi to save data.

**WhatsApp (Android)**: open WhatsApp, Settings, Chats, Chat backup. Choose your Google account, set a schedule such as weekly, and turn off backup over mobile data. These backups count towards your Google storage.
**Check space**: open the Drive app, tap the menu, and see how much of your 15 GB is used. Delete large files you no longer need.

blocks.title: Worked example: applying from a phone
blocks.context: For example, Joy in Calabar is applying for a job that asks for her CV, a certificate and a reference letter as links by email.
steps: She scans her certificate and reference letter with Drive's Scan button and names each file clearly.
She uploads her CV and moves all three into a folder named Job applications.
She shares each file as Viewer with the employer's email address, keeping General access as Restricted.
She sends the email with the three links and a short message saying what each file is.
blocks.result: The employer can open the files, cannot change them, and nobody else can see Joy's documents.

blocks.text: Drive can also make files available **offline**. Press and hold a file and choose Make available offline, so you can open it without data, for example during a power or network outage. Remember that offline copies take space on your phone.

Every few months, open **Shared with me** and the sharing settings of your own important files. Remove people who no longer need access, and change links that were set to Anyone with the link back to Restricted.
Working together in one file

Drive also includes free apps for creating files: **Google Docs** for letters and reports, **Google Sheets** for tables such as a stock list or a contribution record, and **Google Slides** for simple presentations. Several people can work in the same file at once from their phones, and every change is saved automatically. For example, a cooperative treasurer can keep the monthly contribution sheet in Sheets, share it as Viewer with members so everyone sees the same numbers, and give Editor access only to the secretary.
Docs and Sheets keep a **version history**, so if someone deletes something by mistake, the owner can open the file, tap the three dots and restore an earlier version.

takeaways: Drive keeps your files safe online, with 15 GB free shared across Google services.
Use Scan to turn paper documents into clean PDFs.
Share as Viewer by default and keep personal files Restricted.
Back up photos and WhatsApp chats on Wi-Fi.

activity.title: Build your safe document folder
steps: Create a Drive folder called Important documents.
Scan two documents such as a certificate and a receipt and save them there with clear names.
Share one file with a friend as Viewer, then remove their access.
Turn on Google Photos backup on Wi-Fi and set a weekly WhatsApp chat backup.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your Important documents folder and the Manage access screen showing Restricted.

lessons.title: Video calls and online classes on your phone: Meet, Zoom and WhatsApp
objectives: Join a Google Meet, Zoom or WhatsApp video call from a link
Use mute, camera, chat and raise hand controls correctly
Reduce data use during calls and online classes
Protect meetings from strangers and fake meeting links

blocks.text: Video calls let you attend classes, cooperative meetings, job interviews and family gatherings without travelling. On a smartphone you will mostly use three tools: **WhatsApp** for small family or group calls, **Google Meet** and **Zoom** for classes, training and formal meetings.

blocks.name: video-call
blocks.alt: People on a video call on a screen
blocks.caption: With a phone and a link, you can join a class or meeting from anywhere with signal.

blocks.text: Which tool for which meeting

head: Tool
Free version
Best for
rows: Group voice and video calls with up to 32 people
One-to-one calls up to 24 hours; group calls of three or more up to 60 minutes, up to 100 people
Classes and meetings; works with your Google account
Training sessions and events, often run by organisations

blocks.text: Limits on free plans change from time to time, so check the official help pages if a long meeting matters. The organiser's plan sets the limit, not yours, so you can join longer meetings hosted on paid accounts without paying.
Joining from a link

items: Install the Google Meet or Zoom app from the Play Store before the meeting day. Check the developer is Google LLC or Zoom.
Tap the meeting link you received from the organiser. It opens the right app.
Before joining, check your name is shown properly, for example your full name rather than "Samsung A12". In Zoom you can change it in the join screen.
Turn your microphone off before entering, then tap Join or Ask to join.
If there is a waiting room, wait for the host to admit you.

blocks.title: Before every online class
items: Charge phone and check data
Install app in advance
Join five minutes early
Mute on entry
Camera on when asked
blocks.caption: A short routine before each class avoids the most common problems.

blocks.text: The controls you will use

items: **Microphone**: mute when you are not speaking, to stop background noise from generators, children or traffic.
**Camera**: turn it off to save data and battery when it is not needed.
**Chat**: type questions or answers without interrupting the speaker.
**Raise hand**: signals to the host that you want to speak.
**Leave**: the red button ends your part in the call.

blocks.title: Save data on calls
blocks.text: Video calls are among the heaviest uses of data. Switch your own camera off unless you are presenting, close other apps, and use trusted Wi-Fi when you can. In WhatsApp, turn on Use less data for calls in Storage and data settings.

blocks.title: Worked example: a smooth first class
blocks.context: For example, Mercy in Uyo is joining her first WODDI Institute live class on Google Meet at 7pm, using a phone with about 2GB of data left.
steps: At midday she installs Google Meet from the Play Store and checks the developer is Google LLC.
At 6:30pm she charges her phone, closes other apps and sits near the window for a stronger 4G signal.
At 6:55pm she taps the class link, turns off her microphone and camera, and joins.
She uses the chat to answer the facilitator's question and raises her hand once to speak, turning her microphone on and off again afterwards.
After the one-hour class she checks Data usage and sees Meet used a few hundred MB with her camera off.
blocks.result: Mercy joined on time, took part fully and still had most of her data bundle left.

blocks.text: Meeting safety

items: Do not post meeting links publicly on social media; share them only with invited people.
Hosts should use a waiting room or Ask to join, and only admit names they recognise.
Be wary of messages saying "your Zoom needs updating, click here". Update only through the Play Store.
Before turning on your camera, check what is visible behind you, such as documents, addresses or children.

blocks.title: Fake interviews
blocks.text: A "job interview" on video that asks you to pay a fee, install an app from a link, or show your ATM card or BVN on camera is a scam. Genuine employers do not ask for these.

Good online etiquette is simple: join on time, use your real name, mute when not speaking, use the chat for questions, and say goodbye before you leave. These habits make you look professional in class and at interviews.

If your connection drops, do not panic. Rejoin with the same link, and if video keeps freezing, turn your camera off or switch to audio only. Many organisers record classes, so ask whether a recording will be shared if you miss part of it.

Online learning goes beyond live calls. Recorded lessons, quizzes and certificates on platforms such as WODDI Institute let you study at your own pace. Download videos on Wi-Fi when the platform allows it, study in short daily sessions, and keep notes in a notebook or a Google Doc so you can revise without using data.

takeaways: Use WhatsApp for small groups, and Meet or Zoom for classes and formal meetings.
Install apps from the Play Store in advance and join a few minutes early.
Mute when not speaking and turn the camera off to save data.
Keep meeting links private and ignore fake update or interview requests.

activity.title: Practice call
steps: Install Google Meet or Zoom from the Play Store and check the developer.
Create or join a short practice call with a friend or family member.
Practise muting, turning the camera on and off, using chat and raising your hand.
After the call, check Data usage to see how much data it used.
activity.evidence: A screenshot from your practice call (with permission from the other person) and a note of the data it used.

quiz.q: A friend sends you an APK file on WhatsApp for a "free premium" version of an app. What should you do?
options: Install it, because a friend sent it
Turn on Install unknown apps just this once
Do not install it; get apps only from the Play Store
Rename the file before installing
quiz.explain: APKs skip Play Store checks and are a common way to spread apps that steal codes and data.

quiz.q: Rita's phone suddenly shows No service for an hour while her neighbour on the same network has full signal. What is the best first step?
options: Wait until tomorrow
Use another phone to call her network and her bank to block the number and freeze her account
Restart the phone ten times
Post about it on Facebook
quiz.explain: This may be a SIM swap. Calling the network and bank quickly can stop money being moved.

quiz.q: A buyer shows Hauwa a transfer screenshot and an SMS alert, then asks for a refund of "extra" money. How should she confirm payment?
options: Trust the SMS alert
Trust the screenshot
Check the balance inside her own bank app
Ask the buyer to swear
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS can be faked. Only the balance in her own bank app is reliable.

quiz.q: Joy is sharing her certificate with an employer through Google Drive. Which setting is best?
options: Editor, Anyone with the link
Viewer, shared with the employer's email, General access Restricted
Commenter, Anyone with the link
Editor, shared with the employer's email
quiz.explain: Viewer access to a named person lets the employer read it while nobody else can open or change it.

quiz.q: Which loan app sign should make you stop?
options: It is published by a licensed lender and appears on the FCCPC's approved list
It asks for access to all your contacts and photos and has reviews about harassment
It explains its fees clearly
It has a clear customer service address
quiz.explain: Contact and photo access is used by abusive lenders to shame borrowers. Check the FCCPC list first.

quiz.q: Mercy has little data left before a one-hour Google Meet class. What helps most?
options: Keep her camera on the whole time
Turn her camera off unless asked and close other apps
Join from a browser with ten tabs open
Unmute so the host can hear her
quiz.explain: Video is the heaviest use of data, so switching her own camera off saves the most.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement about the internet and the World Wide Web is correct?
options: They are exactly the same thing
The Web is the network of cables; the internet is the websites
The internet is the network; the Web is the pages you open in a browser
Only computers can use the internet
finalQuiz.explain: The internet is the network itself. The Web is one service that runs on it.

finalQuiz.q: Blessing's 30-day bundle finishes in ten days. Data usage shows Play Store used 1.2 GB. What should she change?
options: Set Play Store auto-update to Over Wi-Fi only
Uninstall WhatsApp
Turn off her screen lock
Buy only daily plans
finalQuiz.explain: App updates are large and often hidden. Setting updates to Wi-Fi only stops them eating mobile data.

finalQuiz.q: In the address https://moniepoint.com.verify-now.site/login, who owns the site?
options: Moniepoint
Whoever owns verify-now.site
Google
The Central Bank
finalQuiz.explain: The real domain is the last part before the first single slash: verify-now.site.

finalQuiz.q: Which search is most likely to give only official government results about NIN?
options: NIN please help
NIN site:nimc.gov.ng
"NIN" -gov
NIN Sponsored
finalQuiz.explain: The site: operator limits results to the official website named.

finalQuiz.q: You receive an email from "Access Bank Alert" asking you to confirm your BVN through a link within 24 hours. What is the safest response?
options: Click the link quickly before the deadline
Reply with your BVN to be safe
Do not click; check the real sender address, report it as phishing and contact the bank through its official app or number
Forward it to your friends
finalQuiz.explain: Urgency plus a request for your BVN are classic phishing signs. Use official channels only.

finalQuiz.q: Kunle is emailing a job application. Which is best?
options: No subject, CV attached, no message
Subject with job title and name, short message, CV attached as a clearly named PDF
Subject "hi" and a voice note
The CV pasted as a photo in the body only
finalQuiz.explain: A clear subject, a short message and a well-named PDF make the application easy to read and file.

finalQuiz.q: Which choice gives the strongest protection for a Google account?
options: A short password with symbols, used on every site
A unique passphrase plus 2-Step Verification or a passkey
Writing the password in your WhatsApp status
Using your phone number as the password
finalQuiz.explain: A unique passphrase stops leaks spreading, and a second step or passkey stops stolen passwords working.

finalQuiz.q: Someone on WhatsApp says they sent you a code by mistake and asks you to send it back. What does a two-step verification PIN do in this situation?
options: Nothing at all
It adds a second lock, so even with the SMS code they cannot register your account without the PIN
It deletes your chats
It sends the code to them automatically
finalQuiz.explain: The PIN is needed in addition to the SMS code, which blocks most WhatsApp takeovers. Still, never share the code.

finalQuiz.q: Amaka is at an airport on free Wi-Fi. Which task should she move to mobile data?
options: Reading the news
Watching a downloaded course video
Logging into her bank app to make a transfer
Checking the weather
finalQuiz.explain: Banking and passwords should not go over public Wi-Fi she does not control.

finalQuiz.q: A torch app asks for access to your contacts and location. What should you do?
options: Allow both, apps always need them
Deny them, or uninstall the app and choose one that asks only for what it needs
Allow only contacts
Restart the phone
finalQuiz.explain: Permissions should match the app's purpose. A torch needs neither contacts nor location.

finalQuiz.q: Grace's SIM suddenly says SIM not registered, and she gets an SMS about a SIM replacement she never requested. What should she do first?
options: Wait a day to see if it fixes itself
Use another phone to call her network and her bank immediately
Buy a new phone
Post the problem on Facebook
finalQuiz.explain: These are SIM-swap signs. Fast calls to the network and bank can stop criminals using her OTPs.

finalQuiz.q: Which Google Drive sharing setting is right for a scanned NIN slip sent to one employer?
options: Anyone with the link, Editor
Restricted, shared as Viewer with the employer's email only
Anyone with the link, Viewer
Posted in a public WhatsApp group
finalQuiz.explain: Sensitive documents should be shared only with named people, with the lowest access needed.

capstone.title: My Safe Phone Portfolio
capstone.brief: Produce a short portfolio showing that your phone, accounts and money are set up safely: data-saving settings, a working professional Gmail, two-step verification, cleaned-up passwords, privacy settings, a safe app list and a written SIM-swap emergency card.
steps: Set up data saving: Android Data Saver, WhatsApp media download on mobile data, YouTube quality and Play Store updates on Wi-Fi only. Take screenshots.
Create or tidy your Gmail account with recovery phone and email, run Security Checkup, and send one professional email using the five-part structure.
Change your email password to a four-word passphrase, run Password Checkup, and create a passkey for your Google account.
Turn on 2-Step Verification for Google and a two-step PIN for WhatsApp, and store your backup codes on paper at home.
Complete a privacy tune-up: app permissions, Google Privacy Checkup, WhatsApp privacy and Find My Device. Forget public Wi-Fi networks and secure your hotspot.
Run Play Protect, remove unused apps, and write your SIM-swap emergency card with your network and bank emergency contacts (no PINs or account numbers).
Collect two real phishing or scam messages (personal details hidden) and write the warning signs you found in each.
evidence: Screenshots of the four data-saving settings
Screenshot of Google Security Checkup with no warnings
A copy of your professional email (personal details hidden if needed)
Screenshots showing Google 2-Step Verification on and WhatsApp two-step verification on
Screenshot of WhatsApp Privacy settings and Google Privacy Checkup
Play Protect scan result and list of apps removed
Two analysed scam messages with warning signs listed
